strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing source-scarce LLM evaluation with clear practical relevance
Sound technical approach: alignment mechanism elegantly handles model heterogeneity via model-specific projections and shared MLP
Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 benchmarks with 200+ models, including proper ablations and sensitivity analyses
Insightful spectral analysis (Section 4) rigorously demonstrating that aligned representations capture both item difficulty and task-specific structure using stratification by difficulty
Agreement metric effectively catches error cancellation issues, providing more nuanced evaluation than aggregate MAE
Demonstrates robustness to temporal distribution shift and works effectively with as few as 5 source models
weaknesses: Improvements over GP-IRT baseline are often modest (e.g., GSM8K: 0.763 vs 0.750 Spearman correlation at K=10); gains diminish as K increases, suggesting limited advantage beyond extreme scarcity

Extrapolation phase (Eq. 6-7) uses only single scalar feature despite investing effort in learning rich representations; no justification for why aligned embeddings themselves aren't used as regression features
Method requires access to hidden states, making it inapplicable to closed-source models which are increasingly prevalent; also requires benchmark-specific training of alignment reducing generality

SEED-Bench-2-Plus shows notably degraded performance relative to other benchmarks (Spearman 0.642 at K=10 vs 0.718 for BBH) without adequate explanation of why approach struggles with multimodal tasks

Design choices lack complete justification: consensus embedding averaging discards model-specific information without explanation; dimension dz=32 chosen empirically without sensitivity analysis; clustering algorithm details unclear
Presentation density and complexity of statistical protocols in Section 4 make key insights difficult to extract; connection between representation analysis and downstream task performance unclear

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: efficient LLM benchmarking with limited source models (≤10)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 diverse benchmarks and 200+ models with careful statistical reporting and variance analysis
Rigorous representational analysis (Section 4) with stratified statistical testing, FDR correction, and proper aggregation methods to isolate task structure from difficulty
Extensive ablations examining source pool size, composition, capability range, temporal drift, and coreset scaling
Clear presentation of the three-phase pipeline with effective motivating figures
Data-efficient learning demonstrated through saturation analysis showing performance plateaus at ~15-20 source models
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applies standard representation alignment (model-specific projections + shared MLP), consensus clustering, and ridge regression with no novel algorithmic contributions

Critical soundness concerns: (1) unclear interaction between per-benchmark 70/10/20 train/val/test splits and cross-model evaluation; (2) final layer, final token extraction unjustified with no ablation; (3) claimed d_z=32 based on 99% variance unsubstantiated

Unfair baseline comparisons: metric selection appears post-hoc (MAE favors GP-IRT → introduce Agreement metric favoring REPCORE); no pre-specified metrics; incomplete ablations (Table 4 only K=30); no significance testing

Circular reasoning in representational analysis: MLP trained on correctness prediction, so of course learned representations capture correctness; stratified analysis partially addresses but doesn't eliminate fundamental issue; PCA alignment with difficulty may reflect training objective artifact

Unjustified architectural choices: (1) why train classifier g_φ but discard it?; (2) why use simple scalar feature x_i (Eq. 7) for extrapolation instead of learned embeddings?; (3) why L2-normalize in Eq. 3 with no ablation?; (4) K selection procedure unclear

Restricted applicability: requires hidden state access, excluding commercial models (GPT-4, Claude); limited to reasoning/math/multimodal benchmarks; temporal drift results mixed (better ranking but worse MAE than GP-IRT, contradicting narrative)

Reproducibility gaps: Ridge regularization strength unspecified; MLP training details (optimizer, learning rate, schedule) missing; no code availability mentioned; model generation procedures incomplete (temperature, top-p not specified)
Marginal improvements over competitive baseline: GSM8K K=20 ranking correlation 0.872 vs 0.839 (GP-IRT); improvements sometimes within statistical noise with no significance tests provided
Missing comparisons: no ablation removing supervised training phase; no comparison to domain adaptation alignment methods; no comparison to simpler unsupervised alternatives

Modest effect sizes in analysis: PC1 difficulty correlation ρ≈0.46, task type ε²≈0.54 show substantial overlap; no latent space visualization (t-SNE/UMAP); unclear statistical power with 20 difficulty bins on small benchmarks

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem with clear illustration of existing method limitations in source-scarce regimes
Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 benchmarks and 200+ diverse models with consistent improvements

Rigorous representational analysis (Section 4) with proper statistical corrections revealing that learned representations encode both difficulty and task-specific structure beyond mere performance signals
Extensive ablations validating key design choices (discrete vs continuous representations, source pool sensitivity, model composition effects)
Strong reproducibility with multiple independent runs, explicit train/val/test splits, and comprehensive model specifications
Demonstrated effectiveness with minimal supervision (as few as 5 source models), addressing a real bottleneck for newly released benchmarks
Honest reporting of fidelity metrics (Agreement) that reveal when aggregate metrics (MAE) can mask item-level errors
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (hidden state extraction, alignment projections, clustering) for a new application without introducing novel methodology
Hidden state layer/token selection (final layer, final token) insufficiently justified; no ablation study comparing alternatives despite this being a critical design choice
Bottleneck dimensionality (d_z=32) justified only by effective rank analysis; no sensitivity analysis for robustness to this hyperparameter

Information loss during extrapolation: Phase 3 uses only scalar average correctness feature while Phase 1 learns rich 32-dim representations; Table 2 suggests embeddings/PCs contain complementary signal
Clustering algorithm choice (cosine K-means) not explored; no analysis of sensitivity to cluster count K or comparison with alternative clustering approaches
Computational overhead not addressed: hidden state extraction, alignment training, and clustering costs not quantified relative to baselines; memory requirements not discussed
Limited baseline diversity: missing comparisons to simpler continuous features (logits, attention patterns) and other alignment techniques
Temporal generalization only tested on 30%/70% historical/future split; more severe distribution shifts would better validate applicability to new benchmarks
Improvements on multimodal benchmark (SEED-Bench) sometimes modest; generalization to truly visual/audio-only benchmarks unclear
Stratified analysis uses arbitrary 20 equal-width bins for difficulty; robustness to alternative binning not demonstrated (though extreme p-values suggest stability)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 benchmarks and 200+ models with consistent improvements over multiple baselines
Well-motivated problem identifying genuine limitations of output-based methods in source-scarce regimes
Rigorous interpretability analysis (Section 4) demonstrating aligned representations capture task-specific structure beyond difficulty via spectral decomposition and difficulty-stratified analyses
Extensive ablation studies covering source pool size, model composition, temporal drift, and alternative clustering inputs
Practical efficiency with negligible runtime overhead (0.4%) and modest storage requirements (0.11-1.25GB)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies standard techniques (linear projections, MLPs, k-means, ridge regression) to hidden states rather than proposing novel methods
Contradictory motivation: identifies output-level signals as unreliable yet trains the alignment network using cross-entropy loss on these same binary labels (Eq. 2)

Critical practical limitation: requires hidden state access from source models, preventing use with closed-source/API-only models; Section 6.1 shows 50% adversarial masking degrades Spearman ρ from 0.84 to 0.81
Scope restricted to binary-scored benchmarks only; cannot address continuous metrics, ranking-based evaluation, or other assessment paradigms

Inconsistent experimental framing: dramatic improvements shown at |S|=5 (AnchorPoints 0.640→0.860) but main experiments use |S|=10 where improvements are modest (0.707 vs 0.706 on ARC-Challenge); true source-scarce boundary underexplored

Missing critical ablations: clustering method selection unexplored, consensus embedding uses simple averaging rather than learned weights, embedding dimension d_z=32 set empirically without systematic analysis
Insufficient statistical rigor: limited confidence intervals, no formal significance testing across comparisons, multiple comparisons without correction
